images.filename: Coastwatch lookout station at Gwennap Head - geograph.org.uk - 229825.jpg
images.caption: Coastwatch lookout station at Gwennap Head. This lookout station is high on the cliffs at Gwennap Head, looking out over the sea south of Lands End. These stations used to be manned by HM Coastguard, but now they are maintained by an organisation called Coastwatch which is funded by public contributions. The open door on the right of the building leads to a room with reading and information about the local geography and history, and also explains what Coastwatch is. If you look very closely through the upper window you can see the lookout peering through some powerful binoculars.

images.filename: Cliff west of Hella Point - can you see the faces^ - geograph.org.uk - 230010.jpg
images.caption: Cliff west of Hella Point - can you see the faces? The cliffs around Hella Point are well worn by the harsh conditions on this tip of Cornwall that faces the full brunt of the Atlantic winds and waves. I saw a similar photo for sale as a postcard in Porthgwarra's shop, inviting you to count the number of 'faces' in the cliff. The fissured rounded surface is perfect for this kind of game.

images.filename: Maritime heath at Gwennap Head - geograph.org.uk - 229828.jpg
images.caption: Maritime heath at Gwennap Head. Heathland on top of the granite cliffs, with common heather (calluna vulgaris), bell heather (erica cinerea) and western gorse (ulex gallii) - all stunted by the severe conditions on this exposed headland. The visitors room in the nearby Coastwatch station contains information on the natural history of the headland, including the fact that the gorse is yellow, the common heather pale pink and the bell heather deep pink. It also claims that this is the windiest place on the British mainland, but I don't know if this is factually correct or just supposition! Compare with 71871 in the neighbouring gridsquare.

images.filename: Navigation markers on Gwennap Head - geograph.org.uk - 229831.jpg
images.caption: Navigation markers on Gwennap Head. These two cone-shaped landmarks are there to warn sea vessels of the Runnel Stone - a hazardous rock pinnacle about a mile offshore between Hella Point and Tol Pedn. When at sea the black and white cone should always be kept in sight.. but if it should be completely obliterated by the red cone then the vessel would be on top of the Runnel Stone! A plaque on the far side of the black and white cone reads "THIS BEACON WAS ERECTED BY THE CORPORATION OF TRINITY HOUSE OF DEPTFORD, STROUD, IN 1821." Nowadays the Runnelstone is directly marked by a buoy which emits an eerie moaning sound which can be heard all over this headland. Note: some of this information was taken from a booklet in the visitors' room at the nearby 229825.

images.filename: Coast path on Gwennap Head - geograph.org.uk - 850780.jpg
images.caption: Coast path on Gwennap Head The two daymarks on the right warn shipping of the Runnelstone reef - provided that the black and white marker is not obscured from view by the red one, the ship will be clear of the reef.   If the black and white marker is not visible the ship is too close to the reef.  In the distance can be seen the Gwennap Head coastguard lookout, now operated by the voluntary National Coastwatch Institution.
